summary.text: Writing factorials as their multiples-of-�p contribution times the �p-free product, the proof expands each shifted block modulo �p^{3r}; symmetry of inverses and the vanishing of the sum of squared units give the required �p^{2r}- and �p^r-divisibility of the first two reciprocal sums, so every full block is congruent to the initial one. The even case then follows by cancellation, while for odd indices the gamma duplication formula produces an explicit power of �2, which is matched by an odd/even splitting and cubic product identity before the remaining unit factors are cancelled.

full_proof.text:
We prove the stated congruence under the stated integrality hypothesis. Thus, for each nonnegative integer m, let A_m be the integer whose image in R is a(m). (It is unique, since the embedding of Z into R is injective.) We shall prove

A_{np^r} \equiv A_{np^{r-1}} \pmod {p^{3r}}

for every prime p >= 5, every n>0, and every r>0.

Throughout the proof, p is a fixed prime at least 5 and r>0. All congruences in the main argument take place in the ring

R_r = Z/(p^{3r})Z.

We first establish the p-adic product identities needed in both parity cases.

1. The p-free part of a factorial

Define

psi(m) = 1 if p divides m, and psi(m)=m otherwise,

and

F(M)=product_{1 <= j <= M} psi(j).

Thus F(M) is the product of all integers from 1 through M after every multiple of p has been replaced by 1. Separating the multiples of p from the other factors gives

M! = p^{floor(M/p)} floor(M/p)! F(M).                 (1)

Indeed, the factors divisible by p are p,2p,...,floor(M/p)p, whose product is p^{floor(M/p)} floor(M/p)!, and all remaining factors form F(M). In particular, if M=pq+s with 0<=s<p, then

M! = p^q q! F(M).                                    (2)

Every factor in F(M) is prime to p, so F(M) is a unit modulo every power of p.

For K>=1 and a nonnegative integer m, define v_K(m) in Z/(p^K)Z by

v_K(m)=0 if p divides m,

v_K(m)=m^{-1} if p does not divide m.

This function is multiplicative:

v_K(ab)=v_K(a)v_K(b).                                 (3)

If p divides A, then, modulo p^K,

psi(A+m)=psi(m)(1+A v_K(m)).                          (4)

If p divides m, both sides equal 1. If p does not divide m, the right side is m(1+A/m)=A+m, which is also prime to p because p divides A. Multiplying (4) over a finite interval gives the corresponding product identity.

2. Harmonic sums over complete p-power blocks

We need two divisibility statements. For K>=r, put N=np^r. Then in Z/(p^K)Z,

sum_{0<=m<N} v_K(m)^2 is divisible by p^r,             (5)

sum_{0<=m<N} v_K(m) is divisible by p^{2r}.            (6)

We prove (5) first. Reduce the sum modulo p^r. Each interval of length p^r contributes the same sum, because v_r(ap^r+i)=v_r(i). Therefore it is enough to show

sum_{0<=i<p^r} v_r(i)^2=0 in Z/(p^r)Z.                (7)

The nonzero terms in this sum are indexed by the units modulo p^r, and inversion permutes those units. Consequently the left side equals the sum S of the squares of all units modulo p^r. Multiplication by 2 also permutes the units, because p is odd, and hence S=4S. Thus 3S=0. Since p>=5, 3 is a unit modulo p^r, so S=0. This proves (7), hence (5).

To prove (6), work in Z/(p^K)Z and write

S=sum_{0<=m<N}v_K(m),    T=sum_{0<=m<N}v_K(m)^2.

Because p divides N, reflection m -> N-m, with the endpoints handled using v_K(0)=v_K(N)=0, preserves the sum. For 0<=m<=N one has

v_K(m)+v_K(N-m)=N v_K(m)v_K(N-m).                     (8)

This is immediate if p divides m; otherwise multiply both sides by m(N-m), which is a unit, and use m+(N-m)=N. Multiplying (8) by v_K(m) and rearranging also gives

v_K(m)v_K(N-m)
 =-v_K(m)^2+N v_K(m)^2v_K(N-m).                       (9)

Adding (8) and then using (9), we obtain

2S=-N T+N^2 sum_{0<=m<N}v_K(m)^2v_K(N-m).             (10)

By (5), T is divisible by p^r, while N itself is divisible by p^r. Both terms on the right of (10) are therefore divisible by p^{2r}. Since 2 is a unit modulo p^K, S is divisible by p^{2r}. This proves (6).

3. Products over p^r-blocks

We use the elementary third-order product expansion. In any commutative ring, if X^3=0, then

2 product_i(1+Xw_i)
 =2+2X sum_i w_i
   +X^2((sum_i w_i)^2-sum_i w_i^2).                  (11)

This follows simply by expanding the product: terms of degree at least three vanish, and

2 sum_{i<j}w_iw_j=(sum_iw_i)^2-sum_iw_i^2.

In particular, if

X sum_iw_i=0,   X^2 sum_iw_i^2=0,

then the product is 1, since 2 is invertible.

Apply this in R_r with X=Mp^r and w_i=v_{3r}(i+1), for 0<=i<p^r. Here X^3=0. By (6), the sum of the w_i is divisible by p^{2r}; by (5), the sum of their squares is divisible by p^r. (Shifting the range from 0,...,p^r-1 to 1,...,p^r does not change either sum, because both endpoint terms are zero.) Hence

product_{i=0}^{p^r-1}(1+Mp^r v_{3r}(i+1))=1.          (12)

Now split F(Mp^r) into M consecutive blocks of length p^r. Formula (4) and (12) show that every translated block has the same product as the first block. Therefore

F(Mp^r) = F(p^r)^M in R_r.                            (13)

This is the basic block lemma.

4. Integer factorial formulas for a(m)

We next remove the gamma functions. For an even argument m=2k, all gamma factors are ordinary factorials, and direct substitution gives

a(2k)= (18k)!(4k)!(3k)! / ((9k)!(8k)!(6k)!(2k)!).    (14)

For an odd argument m=2k+1, the duplication formula

Gamma(z)Gamma(z+1/2)=2^{1-2z} sqrt(pi) Gamma(2z)

applied at z=3k+2 and z=9k+5 gives, after cancellation of sqrt(pi),

a(2k+1)
 = 2^{12k+6}(4k+2)!(9k+4)!
   /((3k+1)!(8k+4)!(2k+1)!).                         (15)

For completeness, the two duplication-formula instances say

(3k+1)! Gamma(3k+5/2)
 =(6k+3)! 2^{-(6k+3)} sqrt(pi),

(9k+4)! Gamma(9k+11/2)
 =(18k+9)! 2^{-(18k+9)} sqrt(pi).

Inserting these into the defining ratio gives (15).

Because a(m)=A_m is an integer, equations (14) and (15) may be cleared of their positive factorial denominators as exact identities in Z. This is the only point where the assumed integrality is needed.

5. The even case

Suppose n is even, say n=2n'. Put

k'=n'p^{r-1};

then n'p^r=pk'. Let x=A_{2n'p^r} and x'=A_{2n'p^{r-1}}. Clearing denominators in (14) gives

x (9pk')!(8pk')!(6pk')!(2pk')!
 =(18pk')!(4pk')!(3pk')!,                            (16)

and

x' (9k')!(8k')!(6k')!(2k')!
 =(18k')!(4k')!(3k')!.                               (17)

Apply (2) with zero remainder to every factorial in (16). On its left, the extracted powers of p have total exponent

(9+8+6+2)k'=25k',

and on its right they have exponent

(18+4+3)k'=25k'.

After substituting (17), canceling the common nonzero integer factor p^{25k'} times the denominator in (17), we obtain

x F(9pk')F(8pk')F(6pk')F(2pk')
 =x'F(18pk')F(4pk')F(3pk').                          (18)

Let Phi=F(p^r) in R_r. Since pk'=n'p^r, the block identity (13) gives

F(cpk')=Phi^{cn'}

for every c. Thus (18), reduced modulo p^{3r}, becomes

x Phi^{25n'}=x'Phi^{25n'}.

The element Phi is a unit, so it can be canceled. Hence x=x' in R_r, proving the desired congruence when n is even.

6. Preparations for the odd case: a power-of-two product

Now suppose n is odd. Since p is odd, both np^r and np^{r-1} are odd. Write

np^r=2k+1,       np^{r-1}=2k'+1.                     (19)

Then

2k+1=p(2k'+1).                                        (20)

We require a finite product identity associated with (20). Define

psi_2(m)=1 if p divides m, and psi_2(m)=2 otherwise.

Since p is odd, multiplicativity of the p-free operation gives

psi(2m)=psi_2(m)psi(m).                               (21)

Among 1,...,q exactly floor(q/p) are divisible by p, and therefore

product_{j=1}^q psi_2(j)=2^{q-floor(q/p)}.             (22)

Splitting F(2k) first into its even and odd positions by (21), and alternatively into two consecutive intervals of length k, then using (20) and (22), yields

product_{i=0}^{k-1} psi((2k+1)+(2i+1))
 =2^{2k-2k'} product_{i=0}^{k-1}psi(2i+1).            (23)

Here is the cancellation explicitly. Pairing positions 2i+1 and 2i+2 gives

F(2k)
 =product_{i<k}psi(2i+1)
  ·product_{i<k}psi_2(i+1)·F(k).

On the other hand,

F(2k)=F(k) product_{i<k}psi(k+1+i).

Canceling F(k), and applying (21) to

(2k+1)+(2i+1)=2(k+1+i),

reduces the left side of (23) to the same odd product times

product_{j=1}^{2k}psi_2(j)=2^{2k-floor(2k/p)}.

From 2k+1=p(2k'+1), one has floor(2k/p)=2k', proving (23).

Since p divides 2k+1, formula (4) applied to (23), followed by cancellation of the p-prime odd product, gives in R_r

product_{i=0}^{k-1}(1+(2k+1)v_{3r}(2i+1))
 =2^{2k-2k'}.                                         (24)

7. The special harmonic identities in the odd case

Set x=2k+1=np^r in R_r and abbreviate

A = sum_{i=0}^{k-1}v_{3r}(2i+1),
B = sum_{i=0}^{k-1}v_{3r}(i+1),
A_2=sum_{i=0}^{k-1}v_{3r}(2i+1)^2,
B_2=sum_{i=0}^{k-1}v_{3r}(i+1)^2.

We claim

x(2A+B)=0,       x^2A_2=0,       x^2B_2=0.            (25)

We give the derivation, since these vanishings are the key extra ingredient in the odd case.

The complete range 0,...,2k splits, after shifting the zero endpoint away, into the odd numbers 2i+1 and the even numbers 2(i+1), for 0<=i<k. By multiplicativity (3), and since 2v_{3r}(2)=1, this gives

sum_{m=0}^{2k}v_{3r}(m)=A+v_{3r}(2)B,                (26)

sum_{m=0}^{2k}v_{3r}(m)^2=A_2+v_{3r}(2)^2B_2.        (27)

By (6), the left side of (26) is divisible by p^{2r}; since x is divisible by p^r, multiplication by x annihilates it in R_r. Also

2A+B=2(A+v_{3r}(2)B),

so the first equality in (25) follows.

For the square sums, reflect each odd number 2i+1 across x=2k+1. Its reflected number is the even number x-2(i+1). Squaring the inverse relation (8), or equivalently expanding it, shows that for each i

v(x-2(i+1))^2
 =v(2(i+1))^2
  +x[-2v(2(i+1))^2v(x-2(i+1))
      +xv(2(i+1))^2v(x-2(i+1))^2].                   (28)

After summing, reflection gives an identity of the form

A_2=v(2)^2B_2+xC                                      (29)

for a certain C in R_r.

By (5) and (27), there is c in R_r such that

A_2+v(2)^2B_2=p^r c.                                  (30)

Combining (29) and (30) gives

2v(2)^2B_2=p^r c-xC.                                  (31)

Now x=np^r, x^3=0 in R_r, and p^{3r}=0. Multiplying (31) by x^2 shows

2v(2)^2x^2B_2=0.

Both 2 and v(2) are units, so x^2B_2=0. Equation (29), multiplied by x^2, then gives x^2A_2=0 because x^3C=0. This completes the proof of (25).

8. A truncated-product identity

We use one further elementary algebraic consequence of (11). Let x^3=0 in a commutative ring in which 2 is invertible, and let w_i,z_i satisfy

x(2 sum z_i+sum w_i)=0,
x^2 sum z_i^2=0,
x^2 sum w_i^2=0.                                  (32)

Then

product_i(1+xw_i)
 =[product_i(1+xz_i)]^6 product_i(1+4xw_i).           (33)

To verify this, write y=x sum z_i. From (32), x sum w_i=-2y, and y^3=0. Formula (11) gives

2 product_i(1+xw_i)=2-4y+4y^2,
2 product_i(1+xz_i)=2+2y+y^2,
2 product_i(1+4xw_i)=2-16y+64y^2.

Modulo y^3, direct multiplication gives

2^6(2-4y+4y^2)=(2+2y+y^2)^6(2-16y+64y^2).

Canceling the invertible power 2^7 proves (33).

Apply this with

w_i=v_{3r}(i+1),       z_i=v_{3r}(2i+1),

for 0<=i<k. Conditions (32) are precisely (25). If

E_1=product_{i<k}(1+xv_{3r}(i+1)),
E_4=product_{i<k}(1+4xv_{3r}(i+1)),
P=product_{i<k}(1+xv_{3r}(2i+1)),

then (33) and (24) give

E_1=P^6E_4=2^{6(2k-2k')}E_4.                          (34)

Write k=k'+d; then 2k-2k'=2d, so

E_1=2^{12d}E_4.                                       (35)

9. The odd case

Let x_0=A_{np^r}=A_{2k+1} and x'_0=A_{np^{r-1}}=A_{2k'+1}. Clearing denominators in (15) gives

x_0(3k+1)!(8k+4)!(2k+1)!
 =2^{12k+6}(4k+2)!(9k+4)!,                           (36)

and the analogous identity with k',x'_0. Since p is odd, write

p=2t+1,  so t=(p-1)/2 and 0<=t<p.

From (20) and k=k'+d one checks

3k+1=p(3k'+1)+t,
9k+4=p(9k'+4)+t,
8k+4=p(8k'+4),
2k+1=p(2k'+1),
4k+2=p(4k'+2).                                       (37)

Apply the factorial decomposition (2) to (36), using the remainders in (37). The extracted p-exponent on the denominator side is

(3k'+1)+(8k'+4)+(2k'+1)=13k'+6,

and on the numerator side it is

(4k'+2)+(9k'+4)=13k'+6.

Thus these powers cancel. Substituting the equation belonging to k' and observing

2^{12k+6}/2^{12k'+6}=2^{12d},

we obtain the exact integer identity

x_0 F(3k+1)F(8k+4)F(2k+1)
 =2^{12d}x'_0F(4k+2)F(9k+4).                         (38)

We now evaluate all these F-factors in R_r. Put

Phi=F(p^r),
Psi=product_{i=0}^{k-1}psi(i+1).

Since 2k+1=np^r, the block identity (13) gives

F(2k+1)=Phi^n,
F(4k+2)=Phi^{2n},
F(8k+4)=Phi^{4n}.                                     (39)

Also

3k+1=(2k+1)+k.

Using (4) on the final interval of length k gives

F(3k+1)=Phi^n Psi E_1.                                (40)

Similarly,

9k+4=(8k+4)+k,

and the starting point 8k+4=4(2k+1) is divisible by p. Therefore

F(9k+4)=Phi^{4n}Psi E_4.                              (41)

Insert (39)-(41) and (35) into (38). Its left side becomes

x_0 Phi^{6n} Psi E_1
 =x_0 Phi^{6n}2^{12d}Psi E_4,

and its right side becomes

x'_0 Phi^{6n}2^{12d}Psi E_4.

Every factor being canceled is a unit in R_r: Phi and Psi are products of numbers prime to p, each factor 1+4xv(i+1) in E_4 is congruent to 1 modulo p and hence is a unit, and 2 is a unit because p>=5. Therefore cancellation yields

x_0=x'_0 in R_r.

This is exactly

A_{np^r}\equiv A_{np^{r-1}} \pmod {p^{3r}}

when n is odd.

The even and odd cases exhaust all positive integers n. Hence, for every prime p>=5 and all positive integers n,r,

a(np^r) \equiv a(np^{r-1}) \pmod {p^{3r}},

where the congruence refers to the integer values supplied by the assumed integrality of the sequence.
